source.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Huai Hong; Yi-Ran Zhao; Wei Tang; Yang Deng; Yu Rong; Wenxuan Zhang

page_placements.theme: Neuron importance, monosemanticity and splitting change with language-model scale

record.tranche_reason: The study measures concept-level specialization of MLP value vectors and calls diffuse storage knowledge superposition. This is a conceptual, aggregate-level test related to neuron polysemanticity, not a direct measurement of individual neurons.
record.gate_note: The study measures Parameter Specialization Score (PSS) by masking selected MLP value vectors and comparing concept-specific and general knowledge scores. Its unit is a value vector, not an individual neuron, and its PSS does not directly count neurons responding to unrelated inputs. Results cited from other work are not recorded. PSS and accuracy values used only as inputs to comparisons are recorded only where the paper reports an outcome relevant to specialization.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the superposition framing but measures a different construct. Its Parameter Specialization Score (PSS) is an aggregate accuracy gap after masking the top-k% concept-selected MLP value vectors. It does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, does not count polysemantic neurons, and does not vary capacity, activation function or architecture. Its results therefore bear on no version and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that more capable LLMs store related knowledge in more specialized MLP value vectors, while weaker models spread it diffusely. They find specialization grows with scale, training and concept popularity. They claim fine-tuning experiments show a causal benefit: FT-PV improves accuracy and reduces hallucination.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses concept-related versus irrelevant-question activation contrasts and vector masking to compute an aggregate PSS for language-model knowledge storage; it does not apply the original neuron visualizations or neuron-level inspection in InceptionV1.
record.method_sensitivity: PSS changes with model size, model family, training stage, concept popularity, and vector masking rate. In Figure 3, the general-minus-concept-specific score difference peaks around 5%–20% masking and then declines.

fits_no_version.finding: An aggregate concept-specialization score of MLP value vectors (PSS) is higher in larger, newer and better-performing LLMs. It correlates with SpecWiki accuracy (Pearson 0.92 MCQ, 0.88 OEG), rises with Qwen1.5 and Gemma2 size, and emerges late in OLMo-2 pretraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept-related knowledge is more localized in selected MLP value vectors in more capable, larger and later-trained LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: PSS is higher for more popular (higher-frequency) concepts in LLaMA2-7B and Qwen2-7B (Fig. 5). No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Knowledge localization in MLP vectors increases with concept frequency in pretraining data.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning only the top-activated value vectors (FT-PV) slightly raises PSS and improves accuracy and hallucination metrics compared with full, complementary or random fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted fine-tuning of concept-selected MLP vectors improves knowledge-task performance.

record.problems: The study analyzes value vectors rather than individual neurons and uses an aggregate PSS that does not directly count polysemantic units. Model-family comparisons are observational, and the proposed feature-capacity mechanism is not directly measured. The authors limit their tested models to 14B parameters or smaller. Table 2's LLaMA2 PSS entries are transcribed as printed, although their scale differs sharply from the Qwen2 entries.

untested.parts: Vision models and image inputs are not studied.
No count or share of individual MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no layer-wise comparison.
No manipulation of features relative to neuron count. Superposition is assumed as framing, not tested.
No study of initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
No controlled activation-function or architecture comparison and no polysemantic-neuron share. The fine-tuning setups induce specialization and measure an aggregate score.
No inspection of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No variation of activation range or explanation scoring for individual neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests'/T2 and its V3/V5 labels are not justified. PSS is a masking-based localization score, not a count of neurons with unrelated responses, and nothing varies capacity or architecture under control. Concept-popularity results (Fig. 5) are not in the rows. The LLaMA2 PSS values in Table 2 appear inconsistent in scale with the rest of the paper.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure the share of individual transformer MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare such shares across layers.

It does not count sparse features relative to neuron capacity or directly test whether capacity pressure causes the observed specialization patterns; it analyzes value vectors rather than individual neurons.
Initialization, regularization, training noise, and whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.
It does not isolate activation function or architecture in controlled comparisons, measure the share of polysemantic neurons, or test SoLU or modern convnets.
The study does not inspect canonical polysemantic neurons for a shared feature or related subfeatures.
It does not vary the examined activation range or compare explanation-scoring methods for individual neurons.

relation.reason: The study discusses knowledge superposition in related work and in interpreting low PSS, but does not test any version of the claim.

tranche.reason: PSS is an aggregate accuracy gap after masking concept-selected MLP value vectors. It is a related but different construct from per-neuron response to unrelated inputs. Superposition is used only as framing and interpretation.

source_check.notes: Rows r1-r5 match the text. PSS is a model-level score, averaged over masking rates k=10-50% and over concepts. Value vectors map one-to-one to MLP intermediate units, but no per-neuron polysemanticity share is reported, so cannot_determine and versions none are right. The authors read higher PSS as less knowledge superposition.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Model scale comparisons in Qwen1.5 and Gemma2
reader_labels.reason: PSS rises with model size in both reported families, alongside higher MCQ accuracy (r3–r9); this is consistent with less diffuse knowledge storage at larger scale, but does not establish the proposed feature-to-neuron capacity cause.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Cross-model correlations and OLMo-2 pretraining checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: Specialization is associated with performance and emerges later in training, but these results are aggregate PSS measures and do not directly test capacity pressure or individual neuron mixtures (r1–r2, r18–r20).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported model-family comparisons and vector fine-tuning setups
reader_labels.reason: PSS varies across model sizes and changes across training setups; the authors report FT-PV as improving specialization and knowledge-task performance (r3–r9, r21–r28).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The family comparisons are not controlled architecture or activation-function tests, and the reported outcome is aggregate value-vector PSS rather than a polysemantic-neuron share; the fine-tuning results do not establish that neuron polysemanticity is lowered without a large performance cost (r10–r17, r21–r28).
